faqs[0].answer.sourceText: Start 2-5 minutes before you're due to speak. The calming effects kick in within 60-90 seconds and can last 15-20 minutes. If you're particularly anxious, do a longer session (5 minutes) 30 minutes before, then a quick 60-second refresher right before you go on.

faqs[0].question.sourceText: How far in advance should I start box breathing before a presentation?

faqs[1].answer.sourceText: Pause naturally. Take a sip of water or refer to your notes. Take one slow breath with a longer exhale (4 counts in, 6-8 counts out). This single breath can reset your nervous system enough to continue. For quicker relief mid-speech, try a physiological sigh: two quick inhales through your nose, then one long exhale.

faqs[1].question.sourceText: What if I start panicking during my presentation?

faqs[2].answer.sourceText: Yes, but modify the technique. Shorten the counts to 2-3 seconds, skip the breath holds entirely, and keep the breathing light and quiet. The calming effect comes from the slow, rhythmic pattern, not from deep or forceful breathing. If you feel any discomfort, stop and return to normal breathing.

faqs[2].question.sourceText: Can I do this if I have asthma or breathing difficulties?

faqs[3].answer.sourceText: No. Box breathing is completely invisible when done through the nose. You can practice while sitting in a meeting, standing backstage, or even walking to the podium. Keep your breathing quiet and your body relaxed, no one will know.

faqs[3].question.sourceText: Will people notice I'm doing breathing exercises?

faqs[4].answer.sourceText: Breathing techniques are highly effective for most presentation anxiety, but severe phobias may benefit from additional support like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or gradual exposure practice. Box breathing is an excellent tool to use alongside other strategies. It won't eliminate all fear, but it will give you control over your physical symptoms.

faqs[4].question.sourceText: Does this really work for severe stage fright?

hero.intro.sourceText: Your heart races. Your hands shake. Your mouth goes dry. Stage fright isn't a character flaw. It's your body's ancient survival system misfiring. Box breathing, the same technique used by Navy SEALs and first responders, can interrupt this panic response in under a minute.

hero.subtitle.sourceText: Stop stage fright in 60 seconds with the Navy SEAL method

howTo.steps[0].instruction.sourceText: Step away if possible: a bathroom, hallway, or even your car. If you can't leave, you can do this seated and discreetly.

howTo.steps[1].instruction.sourceText: Sit or stand tall. Drop your shoulders. Unclench your jaw. Place one hand on your belly to feel it rise and fall.

howTo.steps[2].instruction.sourceText: Breathe in slowly through your nose. Let your belly expand, not your chest. Count 1-2-3-4 at a comfortable pace.

howTo.steps[3].instruction.sourceText: Pause gently at the top. Don't clamp down, just let the breath rest. Count 1-2-3-4.

howTo.steps[4].instruction.sourceText: Release slowly through your nose or pursed lips. Feel your belly fall. Count 1-2-3-4.

howTo.steps[5].instruction.sourceText: Pause at the bottom before inhaling again. Stay relaxed. Count 1-2-3-4.

howTo.steps[6].instruction.sourceText: Continue the pattern for 60-90 seconds. Most people feel noticeably calmer after 4 cycles.

howTo.tips[0].sourceText: Practice when you're NOT stressed so the technique becomes automatic

howTo.tips[1].sourceText: Do this in the waiting room, backstage, or while sitting in the audience before your turn

howTo.tips[2].sourceText: If 4-second holds feel too long, start with 3 seconds and work up

howTo.tips[3].sourceText: The technique is invisible to others, no one will know you're doing it

Box breathing is an excellent tool to use alongside other strategies. It won't eliminate all fear, but it will give you control over your physical symptoms.

faqs[4].question.sourceText: Does this really work for severe stage fright?

hero.intro.sourceText: Your heart races. Your hands shake. Your mouth goes dry. Stage fright isn't a character flaw. It's your body's ancient survival system misfiring. Box breathing, the same technique used by Navy SEALs and first responders, can interrupt this panic response in under a minute.

hero.subtitle.sourceText: Stop stage fright in 60 seconds with the Navy SEAL method

howTo.steps[0].instruction.sourceText: Step away if possible: a bathroom, hallway, or even your car. If you can't leave, you can do this seated and discreetly.

howTo.steps[1].instruction.sourceText: Sit or stand tall. Drop your shoulders. Unclench your jaw. Place one hand on your belly to feel it rise and fall.

howTo.steps[2].instruction.sourceText: Breathe in slowly through your nose. Let your belly expand, not your chest. Count 1-2-3-4 at a comfortable pace.

howTo.steps[3].instruction.sourceText: Pause gently at the top. Don't clamp down, just let the breath rest. Count 1-2-3-4.

howTo.steps[4].instruction.sourceText: Release slowly through your nose or pursed lips. Feel your belly fall. Count 1-2-3-4.

howTo.steps[5].instruction.sourceText: Pause at the bottom before inhaling again. Stay relaxed. Count 1-2-3-4.

howTo.steps[6].instruction.sourceText: Continue the pattern for 60-90 seconds. Most people feel noticeably calmer after 4 cycles.

howTo.tips[0].sourceText: Practice when you're NOT stressed so the technique becomes automatic

howTo.tips[1].sourceText: Do this in the waiting room, backstage, or while sitting in the audience before your turn

howTo.tips[2].sourceText: If 4-second holds feel too long, start with 3 seconds and work up

howTo.tips[3].sourceText: The technique is invisible to others, no one will know you're doing it

problem.content.sourceText: When you're about to speak in front of others, your brain can't distinguish between a boardroom presentation and a life-threatening situation. It triggers the same ancient alarm system: adrenaline floods your bloodstream, your heart rate spikes, blood diverts from your brain to your muscles. This was useful when outrunning predators, not so helpful when delivering quarterly results.

science.points[0].explanation.sourceText: Slow, controlled breathing stimulates the vagus nerve, which runs from your brainstem to your abdomen. This activates your parasympathetic nervous system, the 'rest and digest' mode that counteracts fight-or-flight.

science.points[1].explanation.sourceText: When anxious, you tend to over-breathe, depleting CO₂ and causing dizziness and tingling. The hold phases in box breathing normalize CO₂ levels, reducing physical anxiety symptoms.

science.points[2].explanation.sourceText: Counting breath phases occupies your prefrontal cortex, the same brain region that would otherwise be catastrophizing about what could go wrong. You literally crowd out anxious thoughts.

science.points[3].explanation.sourceText: Slow breathing increases heart rate variability (HRV), a marker of stress resilience. Higher HRV means your body can shift more easily between alert and calm states.

solution.content.sourceText: Box breathing (also called tactical breathing or four-square breathing) is used by Navy SEALs, surgeons, and elite performers to regain control under extreme pressure. The technique creates a rhythmic pattern of equal inhales, holds, and exhales that directly counters the panic response.

solution.whyThisPattern.sourceText: The four equal phases (4-4-4-4) give your mind a simple structure to follow, breaking the rumination loop that feeds anxiety. The breath holds allow CO₂ to build up slightly, which paradoxically signals your brain that you're safe enough to pause. You wouldn't hold your breath if you were actually in danger.
